to run its day-to-day operations. Universal Jewelry's products are sourced and imported directly — and the team juggles both retail and wholesale orders, complex pricing structures, and inventory across multiple product lines and fulfillment channels.

Drive productivity with a user-friendly shop-floor interface that allows workers to batch complete tasks while capturing cycle time. Use throughput metrics to identify possible bottlenecks and automatically assign tasks according to worker capabilities, machine capacity, and shift hours.

Gain clarity on future inventory needs by factoring in sales velocity, raw material required for final products, and production lead time. Receive automated alerts for stock-outs, overstock, or expiring materials, and leverage real-time data to adjust schedules or resource allocation without disrupting overall workflow.
Pinpoint Product Costing

Tailor’s retail manufacturing system accurately tracks production costs — even rolling up expenses from multi-tier sub-assemblies and factoring in outsourced production steps. Coupled with Tailor’s Inventory Management solution—which handles complex material costs like landed cost, freight, duty, and various pricing methods—you gain real-time product margins to optimize your bottom line.
Plug & Play integrations for your production workshop

Shorter production cycle times, fewer material shortages, clearer margin visibility, and cleaner handoffs between purchasing, shop floor, and fulfillment — because data lives in one composable model instead of scattered sheets.
How is Tailor priced for Manufacturing, and what drives total cost?

Pricing scales with the modules and automation depth you enable (BOMs, work orders, costing, inventory, procurement). You pay for platform capability and usage, not per user; implementation and support are included.

We start with one flow (e.g., BOM → work order tracking) in weeks, then layer routing, costing, capacity, or variance logic. You provide process definitions and data; we configure schemas, events, and guardrails — phased rollout is standard.

Composable blocks for multi‑level BOMs, work order lifecycle, material allocation, routing steps, production costing, variance capture, and exception alerting. Extend with events, pipelines, or state machines as needs grow.

Connect to commerce demand (Shopify, Amazon), inventory and procurement, shipping (ShipStation), finance (QuickBooks, NetSuite sync), quality/MES via open API, and data/BI (Snowflake). Event-driven sync keeps status and material movements current — keep existing tools and retire later if desired.

Role and record-level access, environment separation, audit trails on BOM/routing and cost changes, encrypted in transit and at rest, and resilient event architecture. Built to align with modern frameworks (e.g., SOC 2) with human review where precision matters.

Raymond Custom Tailoring Case Study
Warehouse Design Consulting

Strategy Implementation: The company was seeking retail consulting services to implement a new business model focused on manufacturing hubs directly for the end user and e-tailoring. Raymond Apparel Ltd. required standardization and streamlining of operations, as well as IT integration for the new model.

YRC also assisted the Raymond team with the standardization of garment production. Raymond was keen to take the online route and there were no standard measurements for styling, customized trims and more across the various franchise retail outlets of the company. YRC helped the Raymond team to adapt to online models and evolved garment manufacturing SOPs.

For Raymond’s unique e-tailoring service, SOPs in terms of specifics and workflows were incorporated right from the receipt of the order to the manufacturing of the product and the final delivery of the apparel.

Right from reports generated at different levels and designations to reporting formats for everyone from the head tailor to the stylist, YRC worked on mapping operations, developing operating manuals and engaging with the team to facilitate franchise management for manufacturing hubs. Going online was one part of the challenge; managing its strategic implications was another.
